hook.text: WWII planes returned with bullet holes in the wings. The military reinforced the wings. Abraham Wald said: wrong.

buildup.text: The planes that didn't return had holes in the engines. Reinforcing wings was studying survivors, not victims.

discovery.text: Survivorship bias: we see what survived and ignore what didn't, drawing wrong conclusions from the visible.

twist.text: Business advice from billionaires ignores the millions who did the same things and still failed.

climax.text: To think clearly, always ask: what am I not seeing? Who dropped out? What data is missing?

punchline.text: The dead can't tell you why they didn't survive.

quiz.question: What is survivorship bias?
options: Drawing conclusions only from what survived, ignoring failures

details.summary: Survivorship bias occurs when we study only the winners and ignore the losers who did the same things but failed. This creates a distorted picture of what leads to success. The famous example is Abraham Wald studying bullet holes on returning planes and armoring the places without holes.
details.whyItMatters: Survivorship bias makes success look more predictable and replicable than it actually is. It corrupts business advice, self-help, and historical analysis.
takeaways: Studying only winners distorts your understanding of success
The missing data from failures is often more informative
Always ask: where are the ones that did not survive?

faq.question: What is the Abraham Wald plane story?
faq.answer: During World War II, the military wanted to armor planes where bullet holes clustered on returning aircraft. Wald realized the holes showed where planes could take damage and survive. The places without holes were where planes got hit and never returned. They armored those areas instead.

faq.question: How does survivorship bias affect business advice?
faq.answer: Business books study successful companies and attribute their success to specific practices. But many failed companies used identical practices. Without studying failures, you cannot distinguish what actually caused success from what was merely present during it.
